items.body: China And St. Augustine - Gavekal Research China And St. Augustine Louis-Vincent Gave Gavekal Research | 23 Oct 2026 Back in the summer of 2015, the Chinese government decided that equity markets had risen too far, too fast. The rug was pulled from under margin lending and various restrictions were put in place that brought the unfolding raging equity bull market to an abrupt end. By January 2024, the Chinese government reversed course and decided that Chinese equity prices had fallen far enough. Beijing intervened in the market (see Chinese Policies And Chinese Equities ) and put a floor under domestic markets. Equities duly rallied, delivering very solid returns for 2024 and 2025. However, over the past year, Chinese equity market returns have been fairly dismal. In fact, Chinese equity markets have now fallen for 10 consecutive weeks, a feat they had never achieved before. This in spite of the fact that (a) excitement over all things “artificial intelligence” has been a key driver of global equity market performance and that (b) China is one of the few countries outside of the US actually registering notable gains on the AI front. items.title_en: What’s the Renminbi Got to Do With it? | Council on Foreign Relations
items.summary_en: A closer look at the impact of China’s currency on China’s export growth.
items.body: Council on Foreign Relations Articles By experts and staff Updated October 11, 2026 12:00 a.m. Brad W. Setser CFR Expert Whitney Shepardson Senior Fellow There is an argument—made in the recent Geneva Report and by various former IMF officials —that China’s current export surge is the simple consequence of the housing downturn and the resulting weakness in Chinese internal demand.* The weakness in the RMB in this story is entirely incidental to the increase in exports, which is, more or less, a mechanical response to weak internal demand. Cannot sell excavators at home? Export them. Built more modern car capacity than your internal market supports ? Export that too… The fall in the nominal RMB over the course of 2022 and the first half of 2023 in nominal and read terms was simply a function of domestic macroeconomic weakness, and a growing rate differential. It wasn’t an active policy choice by China’s central bank. Now, some might note that China’s currency doesn’t always move with rate differentials. items.author: Brad Setser
items.title_en: De-reservification, Not De-dollarization | Council on Foreign Relations
items.summary_en: The world isn’t moving away from the dollar. It is shifting its dollars from traditional reserves to state banks, pension funds, and other quasi-sovereign investors.
items.body: Council on Foreign Relations By experts and staff Published September 15, 2026 8:37 a.m. Brad W. Setser CFR Expert Whitney Shepardson Senior Fellow This is a joint blog with Alex Etra , Senior Macro Strategist and head of Flow of Funds at Vanda Research . The IMF’s data on the currency composition of foreign exchange (FX) reserves is scrutinized carefully for any signs that the world is shifting way from the dollar. Yet it doesn’t really matter that much if the dollar’s share of reserves has shifted from 56.5 percent to 57 percent. The ink-to-impact ratio of the quarterly reporting on the latest COFER data is all off. Neither the stock of global reserves nor the stock of dollar reserves has changed much in the last ten years. The action is elsewhere. China’s state banks (per the Bank of International Settlements) have almost as many foreign assets as the central bank (PBOC). Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund (GPIF) has almost as many foreign assets ( $986 billion ) as the government has FX reserves ($1.1 trillion at the end of August). items.author: Rhodium Group
items.title_en: As Europe Dithers, the Cost of Derisking from China Rises
items.summary_en: The cost of confronting China will be high. But the cost of waiting—for Europe’s economy, security, and sovereignty—could be far higher.
items.body: In March 2023, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called on Europe to unite behind a policy of economic derisking from China. In a speech in Brussels, she warned about Europe’s deepening dependencies on Chinese rare earths, called for more robust trade measures to protect European industry from unfair competition and for new tools to restrict the flow of sensitive technologies to China. More than two and a half years later, it is clear that her warning has gone largely unheeded. Today, Europe is more dependent on critical inputs from China than ever before. China’s export restrictions on critical minerals and chips produced by the Chinese-owned Dutch firm Nexperia have hit European companies in the auto, medical, and defense sectors in recent months, laying bare Europe’s failure to derisk. EU trade defense instruments cover less than 10% of imports from China despite evidence of systemic state support for Chinese companies and an economic model that has relied for years on flooding global markets with cheap goods . Efforts to restrict the flow of artificial intelligence, quantum, and chip technologies to China have stalled amid resistance from European member states

items.summary_en: Rhodium Group is a founding member, with Rhodium Partner Kate Larsen appointed as Director of Data and Analysis of the NEIS Center.
items.body: This week marked the launch of the New Energy Industrial Strategy Center, a new hub dedicated to harnessing advanced energy technologies to strengthen key industries vital to broader economic and national interests. The New Energy Industrial Strategy (NEIS) Center is building a global network of researchers, policymakers, and private sector stakeholders who are advancing industrial strategies that leverage advanced energy systems to support the industries needed for growing, security-conscious nations. The NEIS Center is hosted by RMI and supported by The William and Flora Hewlett Foundation. Rhodium Group is a founding member, with Rhodium Partner Kate Larsen appointed as Director of Data and Analysis of the NEIS Center. Data and analytics from Rhodium’s Global Clean Investment Monitor and China Cross-Border Monitor will be critical inputs for decision-makers navigating this new era of clean energy competition. news_items.title_en: Novel idea: Thailand, Vietnam take books on the road in reading drive | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Two independent publishers travel through regional provinces, offering discounted titles to spark curiosity and connect local communities.
news_items.body: Tran Dai Thang spotted two young people who had picked up their drinks at a pop-up cafe beside his travelling bookstore and were about to leave, so he called them over. One of them said they did not read books, Thang recalled. But he kept the conversation going and eventually persuaded the visitor to buy a book for 10,000 dong (US$0.40) – heavily discounted from its original price of 45,000 dong. For Thang, an artist and publisher, the small sale mattered far less than the fact that someone who said they did not read had chosen to pick up a book. “Who knows, it might be the start of a new habit,” he said. Thang, 53, is spending a year travelling across Vietnam in a truck with his “Books To Every Home” project, also known as “Roaming Turtle”. In neighbouring Thailand, a similar book truck named “Somelee” (Cotton) is pursuing an equally ambitious mission: visiting all 77 provinces to take literature beyond Bangkok and the country’s other urban centres. Their goal goes beyond selling books. news_items.title_en: Law enforcement alerted to firm offering LGBTQ surrogacy services in Hong Kong | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Mainland Chinese influencer says he helped gay couples with the birth and documents of their children by bringing their surrogates to the city.
news_items.body: Hong Kong’s regulator for in vitro fertilisation (IVF) has referred a case to law enforcement agencies after a mainland Chinese influencer was suspected of offering to bring non-local surrogate mothers of LGBTQ parents to give birth in the city. Tan Zubiao, also known as Berlin Sun, had set up a company in the city and advertised on social media commercial surrogacy services for LGBTQ couples, according to Hong Kong media. Tan and his foreign husband, who have two children through surrogacy, were deported from Taiwan’s Kaohsiung last Thursday after being fined NT$200,000 (HK$48,109) for breaching Taiwan’s Medical Care Act by offering assisted-reproductive services. In a written reply to the South China Morning Post on Sunday morning, Hong Kong’s Council on Human Reproductive Technology said commercial surrogacy arrangements and the distribution of related advertisements were prohibited under the city’s Human Reproductive Technology Ordinance. “The Department of Health has referred the case to the council. After seeking legal advice, the council has referred the case to law enforcement agencies for follow-up action,” it said. The SCMP has reached out to Hong Kong police for comment.

With less than two weeks until election day on November 3, though, Representative Mike Collins, the Republican candidate, faces an uphill battle in a state that was once a Republican stronghold. news_items.body: “I think about quitting all the time,” says Jordan Leung, known to his Instagram followers as @69ranch. Leung recently returned to Hong Kong from his base in New York, taking a couple of weeks to spend time with family and recover from jet lag ahead of his “Back to Work” tour shows in Whampoa in October. Originally planning to perform one show each in English and Cantonese on October 17 and 18, the comedian added an extra Cantonese show on the final day thanks to overwhelming demand. news_items.title_en: Will China’s 4 peace principles for tackling African conflicts work? | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Beijing seeks to safeguard billions in regional infrastructure and economic investments while hewing to its pledge of non-interference.
news_items.body: Beijing has a formula for tackling African conflicts and hot-button issues, and during a meeting this month with Togolese leader Faure Gnassingbe, Chinese President Xi Jinping outlined it in four principles linking peace to development. The principles entail focusing on African-led security free from outside intervention; upholding sovereignty and UN Charter principles; rejecting force and sanctions and favouring ceasefires through dialogue; and focusing on both immediate security concerns and long-term development. Asked on Monday whether the principles could be applied to northern Ethiopia and heightened tensions with neighbouring Eritrea, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said they offered “practical guidance” for the Horn of Africa. Days later, a joint statement following a meeting between Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and his Djiboutian counterpart, Abdoulkader Houssein Omar, said China would continue to play a constructive role in mediating regional disputes through its existing Horn of Africa peace-and-development initiative, subject to the wishes of the countries concerned. news_items.title_en: Will AI-powered open-door vending machines reshape Hong Kong’s retail landscape? | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Smart coolers offer seamless grab-and-go convenience but local operators say city’s distinct economic factors may stall widespread adoption.
news_items.body: Sherry Shum has embraced a new shopping routine after finding a smart vending machine near her home in Chai Wan. The 37-year-old retail worker uses her phone to scan a QR code, opens the smart machine’s door, picks up a bottle of Coca-Cola, an oolong tea and a pack of potato chips, closes it and walks away with HK$60 (US$7.70) worth of goods. The whole process is so seamless that the only time she spends is deciding what to buy. The moment Shum takes an item from the shelf, the machine detects the product based on its appearance and debits her account. Once she shuts the door, the bill is settled via the payment method she selected before opening it. “I buy things basically every day … I can grab multiple items at once after just opening the door,” she said. “The open-door machines are more convenient because you do not have to wait for items to drop one by one from traditional machines that sometimes get stuck.” For decades, vending machines have evolved from simple dispensers of bottled or canned drinks into smart retail points that combine digital payments and data-driven consumer insights. news_items.summary_en: Even as the region’s economic downturn is expected to worsen, Gulf states are slated to spend tens of billions of dollars on infrastructure.
news_items.body: Before the outbreak of the war triggered by the US-Israeli attack on Iran in February, the Gulf monarchies were living the prosperity dream that was the envy of the world. Their hydrocarbon-fuelled economies were glitzy oases of growth, inoculated from the conflict in Gaza that had rocked other parts of the Middle East for several years. Underpinned by decades-old US security guarantees and conflict mediation by billionaire sheikhs, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar cultivated images as peaceful lands of opportunity as they invested staggering amounts of money in economic diversification programmes. Backed by sovereign wealth funds with trillions of dollars invested mostly in the West, these leading states of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) embarked on transformative programmes to reposition their economies amid the global transition away from oil and gas. Similar diversification initiatives were also happening in Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain, the other three GCC members. news_items.title_en: Singapore tells suppliers to ‘honour commitments’ amid Indonesia’s gas cut | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the government would explore nuclear power and boost global partnerships for energy security.
news_items.body: Singapore expects all parties who have signed commercial contracts for gas supplies to “honour their commitments”, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Sunday after Indonesia cut its exports. Speaking at the People’s Action Party (PAP) convention, Wong added that Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests. Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore on Saturday. Indonesia’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said the move was to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said the reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet of gas a day amounts to less than 2 per cent of Singapore’s total daily gas demand. About 95 per cent of Singapore’s electricity is generated using natural gas and it imports a significant amount of this gas through pipelines from Indonesia. “The gas supplies are covered by commercial contracts. We expect all parties to honour their commitments and Singapore’s gas importer will take the necessary steps to protect its rights and interests under these contracts,” Wong said. news_items.title_en: ‘Mum, good’: Chinese woman wakes vegetative daughter-in-law after 17 years of care | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Xuan feeds Xu liquid food spoonful by spoonful, taking an hour per meal, and turns her over 10 times daily to prevent bedsores.
news_items.body: A woman in eastern China has been devotedly caring for her daughter-in-law for 17 years, ever since she fell into a vegetative state, moving social media users. The younger woman, surnamed Xu, fell into a vegetative state in 2009 after being struck by a truck in her village in Qingyun county, Shandong province. The accident happened just one month after she got married, Shandian News reported. Since then, her mother-in-law, Xuan Fengying, has cared for her around the clock. “She married my son, so she’s my child. How could I abandon her?” the 68-year-old Xuan was quoted as saying. Xuan fed Xu liquid food one spoonful at a time, and each meal took an hour. She also helped Xu turn over more than 10 times a day to prevent bedsores. Other caregiving tasks included washing Xu after she became incontinent and regularly massaging her muscles. Xuan also talked to Xu about news from the family and their village, played her favourite songs, and repeatedly called her name. Several years ago, Xu miraculously emerged from the vegetative state. news_items.title_en: Fandom vs flag: why young Chinese embrace Japanese pop culture but reject war-era symbols | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: For many on the mainland, the recent rising sun flag incident and controversies like it show a fondness for anime and manga only goes so far.
news_items.body: Young Chinese people enjoy Japanese pop culture such as anime and music, but many draw a firm line at symbols of Japanese militarism. That line was tested recently at Moscow State University, where Chinese students confronted a classmate wearing Japan’s rising sun flag in class and called for his repatriation, state-run newspaper Global Times reported on Sunday. Many countries, including China, view the flag as a symbol of Japanese militarism and aggression. Japan’s Self-Defence Forces still use the flag today. The October 14 incident sparked an online backlash against the Chinese student and praise for those who reported him, following commentaries by People’s Daily, the Communist Party’s official newspaper, and the People’s Liberation Army. “A disgrace to the Chinese people,” read one of the top comments under a post by Jun Zhengping, a social media account run by the PLA. news_items.title_en: Why more Japanese women are choosing ‘silver divorce’ after decades of marriage | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: As children leave home and with changing pension rules, more older Japanese women are choosing to walk away from distant marriages.
news_items.body: Ayumi lives alone in a spacious suburban house originally bought to raise a family, her two cats now her only full-time companions. Her two daughters have grown up and left home, and her husband of more than two decades moved out nearly a year ago as they finalise a divorce. For the 62-year-old Kawasaki resident, who spoke on condition that her surname be withheld, this was not how she envisioned her later years. “He worked very long hours, including on weekends, and I was always busy taking care of the house and raising the children,” Ayumi said. “I think we worked well as a team at the beginning, but somewhere along the way, we just stopped talking like we had before.” The marriage had its fair share of ups and downs – financial stress during their daughters’ university years and the deaths of their respective parents. news_items.body: Hong Kong’s civil service has long enjoyed a reputation for efficiency, professionalism and probity. Outside the general and administrative grades, many civil servants spend much of their careers in relatively specialised areas of responsibility. A youth group attributed the increase to greater reporting driven by heightened mental health awareness, but also students struggling to distinguish playful jokes from bullying. The bureau told the Legislative Council in 2023 that the number of cases involving school bullying, including cyberbullying, from the 2019-20 to 2021-22 school years was 411, 306 and 413 respectively. The average number for these three school years was 377. The figures were based on information contained in the bureau’s annual questionnaire surveys on guidance and discipline cases in schools. Some 200 firefighters were mobilised for the operation at the Kehlsteinhaus residence on a summit above Obersalzberg in southern Germany that draws some 350,000 visitors a year, according to Bavarian state authorities. news_items.body: Police have arrested a 34-year-old man who allegedly mixed rat poison into food left for stray cats in a Kowloon park and was found in possession of a knife. Officers arrived at the scene and seized a packet of suspected rat poison and a fruit knife measuring around 14cm (5.5 inches) in length from the man. “Following a preliminary investigation, the man was arrested on suspicion of cruelty to animals and possession of an offensive weapon and is currently being detained for further investigation,” police said. The Sham Shui Po district crime squad is handling the investigation. Animal welfare volunteers said they first discovered someone appearing to poison food and water left for stray cats last month. A social media user said he installed a surveillance camera on a tree in the park and realised the suspect poisoned food and water at around 3am every Saturday. news_items.title_en: Saudi strikes kill 11 in Yemen as Houthi missiles target Saudi cities | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Houthi media reported a series of ‘Saudi enemy air strikes’ targeting Sanaa, shortly after the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two missiles.
news_items.body: Houthi media reported that Saudi strikes killed 11 people in Yemeni capital Sanaa on Saturday, shortly after the Saudi-led coalition fighting them said it had intercepted two missiles targeting Saudi cities. The Houthis’ Al-Masirah outlet reported a series of “Saudi enemy air strikes” targeting Sanaa, including one on a house that killed at least four people and wounded several others. A separate strike at a residence building for cement factory workers in the Sanaa governorate killed six women and one child and wounded three others, the broadcaster said. Yemen’s civil war, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis against the Saudi-supported and internationally recognised government, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022, but erupted again in July as the wider Middle East war roiled the region. The strikes in Yemen came after the Saudi-led coalition announced it had intercepted two missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif and Yanbu, in the kingdom’s west. Earlier, Riyadh’s civil defence agency broadcast warnings of “potential danger” for four western regions, including Taif and Yanbu as well Mecca, home to Islam’s holiest city, and Yanbu. The alerts were all rescinded minutes later.

news_items.title_en: 2 projector stands removed from controversial Peak lighting project after outcry | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Two large metal stands removed following visit by tourism commissioner, lawmaker and councillor to site.
news_items.body: Parts of two installations in a controversial lighting project along a walking trail on The Peak have been removed, days after Hong Kong’s tourism authorities pledged to balance the community’s needs and said the scheme was not “set in stone”. The removals came hours after Commissioner for Tourism Ann Chan Wai-yan inspected the site on Saturday morning with a lawmaker and a district councillor, following an outcry from residents who accused the Hong Kong Tourism Board of removing trees and flowers to make way for the installations. When the South China Morning Post visited The Peak late on Saturday afternoon, two large metal stands that had held industrial-grade projectors had been removed, leaving only their grey foundational blocks and some bolts, which were not cordoned off. A security guard near the park on the Harlech Road and Lugard Road circular walk confirmed that the two structures had been removed that afternoon. But a smaller metal stand with a projector remained cordoned off near a pavilion. The guard said it had been tested but was not yet fully operational. news_items.title_en: China’s J-20 stealth jet designers plan to put powerful radar into aircraft wing | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: Military aircraft designers propose a wing-mounted early-warning radar to expand coverage during air combat.
news_items.body: Fighter jets typically house their main radars behind a radome in the nose, while conventional airborne early-warning aircraft often carry large radar arrays in prominent structures above the fuselage. Although aircraft wings offer a large surface area, their relatively thin cross-sections leave limited internal space for radar equipment. Top Chinese military aircraft designers have now proposed a revolutionary method to integrate large antenna arrays into aircraft wings, using flight manoeuvres and coordinated formations of unmanned aircraft to expand radar coverage. The design was outlined in a study published online on October 10 in the peer-reviewed Chinese journal Measurement & Control Technology, which presented wing-mounted radar as a new approach to building multifunctional, high-performance airborne early-warning systems. “Wing-mounted early-warning radar is a new type of mission payload designed to meet the early-warning needs of distributed air combat,” researcher Ren Yunsong and his team wrote, describing the concept as “a new pathway” to developing systems with strong detection capabilities. news_items.title_en: Longevity-first healthcare takes spotlight at Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit | South China Morning Post
news_items.summary_en: The event explores innovative breakthroughs and policies emphasising prediction and prevention to help people lead longer, healthier lives.
news_items.body: Issues affecting ageing populations worldwide will form the core of discussions for policymakers and health industry leaders gathered at the Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit, with a particular emphasis on how practising prediction and prevention can help ensure life is lived to its fullest. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has positioned itself as a global leader in transformative healthcare policy, and Dr Asma Al Mannaei, executive director of the health life science sector at the Department of Health – Abu Dhabi, regards the summit as an opportunity to share how those policies are playing out in real time. “Precision medicine is at the heart of it,” Al Mannaei explains, adding that the key to ensuring better health is “understanding each person’s risk through their genome, their biomarkers and their daily life, then acting early.” The Abu Dhabi Future Health Summit is the flagship event of the Future Health platform, the UAE capital’s year-round initiative to promote global collaboration and transformative health innovation.
